planting.note: Set out nursery-grown plants after the last frost, since this Madeira cliff endemic is damaged by hard freezes and needs a full growing season to bulk up its rosette before flowering.

directions: This monocarpic cranesbill forms an enormous rosette of deeply divided, palm-sized leaves on a thick woody stem before sending up a branched flowering dome of hundreds of magenta-pink, dark-eyed blooms, usually in its second or third year, after which the plant dies. Grow it in well-drained soil in full sun near the coast or light afternoon shade in hotter inland gardens, and protect it from frost and strong wind, which can snap the brittle stem. It tolerates poor rocky soil and some drought once established but looks best with regular moisture during active growth. Allow self-sown seedlings to replace the parent plant, since it will not resprout after flowering.

planting.note: Plant in spring once frost danger has passed so the woody-based rosette has a full season to establish before its first flowering flush.

directions: A close relative of the giant Madeira cranesbill, this species forms a smaller, more shrub-like clump of glossy, deeply lobed leaves topped with loose clusters of magenta flowers over a long bloom season. It is somewhat longer-lived than Geranium maderense, often persisting a few years and reseeding readily rather than dying immediately after its first flowering. Give it well-drained soil, full sun on the coast or part shade inland, and shelter from hard frost and desiccating wind. It is easy from seed and often behaves as a reliable short-lived perennial in mild gardens.

planting.note: Transplant in spring into sharply drained soil so the rosette can develop through the growing season; this cliff-dwelling species cannot tolerate wet, cold roots or frost.

directions: This rare Madeira endemic in the bellflower family forms a coarse, lettuce-like rosette of thick, toothed leaves for one to several years before sending up a tall branched spike densely packed with yellow bell-shaped flowers, after which the rosette dies. In the wild it grows wedged into cliff crevices, so garden plants need extremely sharp drainage, lean soil, and full sun, with minimal supplemental water once established. It is strictly frost-tender and is really only practical outdoors in near-frost-free coastal or Mediterranean-type climates, or as a container specimen moved under cover for winter elsewhere. It remains uncommon in cultivation and is grown mainly by specialist exotic-plant and rare-seed sources.
